transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor... I'm here because things at the warehouse have gotten... well, they're not right. The routing system, see, it isn't just a normal computer to me anymore. I know it's been marking my moves. Every time I'm on the floor, it's sending these messages right through the hand scanners to push me out. Just because I'm one of the old hands. 

I’ve been driving those industrial trucks since before they even had screens in the cabs. Back then, we used paper slips. Actually, I remember this one time, my old supervisor—this guy named Gary, had this awful handlebar mustache—he dropped a whole stack of routing slips into a puddle of hydraulic fluid. We spent three hours trying to read the smudged ink. Gary ended up moving to Toledo... or was it Dayton? I can't quite recall. Anyway, he had a brother in roofing, made pretty good money doing shingles. 

But yeah, now it's all computerized, and I just know that system is talking through the scanners to get rid of me.
How long have you felt that the routing system and scanners have been specifically targeting you like this—days, weeks, or longer?

Well, let's see... the voices from the system, and knowing exactly what those scanners are up to... it's been going on for a while now. I'd say about a year and eight months. Around the time they did that big software update, actually. They brought in these IT guys, young kids, mostly. One of them had this bright green lanyard, and he kept chewing on the end of it while he stared at the monitors. I remember thinking, "Kid, you're gonna swallow a piece of plastic." My nephew, Tommy, he swallowed a quarter once when he was five. My sister was beside herself, rushed him right to the ER. They just told her to wait for it to pass, you know? Tommy's 30 now, works in insurance. Sells life policies mostly, out in Omaha. He says the winters there are brutal, worse than here. But yeah, about a year and eight months since the system started coming after me.

During this past year and eight months, have you also noticed periods of feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or low in energy, or on the other hand, unusually elated, full of energy, or needing much less sleep than usual?

Well, it's funny you ask about feeling low, because... yeah. I've been feeling just completely drained, like a heavy wet blanket is on me. Sad, hopeless... all of it. Honestly, it's been going on even longer than the scanner stuff. I'd say about two years and a month now. It started right after they messed with my shift schedule. They moved me to the swing shift, which just wrecks your sleep. 

My buddy Carl, he worked the swing shift down at the bottling plant for ten years. He said it ruined his marriage. His wife, Linda, she was a sweetheart, made the best potato salad. She used a little bit of mustard in it, not too much, just enough for a tang. She got the recipe from her grandmother who came over from Germany. Or maybe Austria? Somewhere over there. Anyway, Carl couldn't stay awake during the day to do things with her, and eventually, she just packed up and went to stay with her sister in Florida. Boca Raton, I think. Beautiful weather down there, but the humidity... I couldn't handle it. I went to Orlando once in August, and I felt like I was breathing soup. 

But yeah, I haven't had any of that high energy stuff you mentioned. Just this deep, heavy sadness for over two years now. It really wears a guy down.
Was there any stretch of time in the last couple of years when your mood felt back to normal—not sad or drained—but you still believed the system and scanners were targeting you?

Well, actually... yeah, there was. Sometime last year, I think it was. The heavy feeling lifted for a bit. I started eating better, even talking a little more to the guys in the break room. They had this new vending machine put in, one of the ones with the glass front where you can watch the coil turn. I used to buy those little powdered donuts, the ones in the white bag? My daughter used to love those when she was little. We'd go fishing down by the creek, and she'd get powdered sugar all over her little overalls. She works in real estate now, out in Seattle. Houses out there are crazy expensive, I don't know how anyone affords it. She sold a house last month that was just a two-bedroom, but it went for over a million. Can you believe that? A million dollars for two bedrooms. 

But anyway, even though my mood was better and I was eating those donuts, for several weeks I was still hearing the dispatch calling my number over the speakers when no one else was around. And I still knew, without a doubt, that the routing system was tracking my every move. The mood got better, but the scanners... they never stopped watching.
During that stretch last year when your mood felt better, about how many weeks or months did that improved mood last before the sadness returned?

Well, let's see... how long did it last? I'd say my mood was better for about three, maybe four months. Yeah, a solid stretch where the heavy feeling eased up some. I was eating a bit more, like I said, talking to the guys in the break room, getting those powdered donuts. But even during those months, you know, for several weeks in there, I still heard dispatch calling my number over the speakers when the floor was empty. And I still knew the routing system was tracking me. 

It's funny how time works, isn't it? Three or four months can feel like a lifetime when you're waiting for something, but it goes by in a flash when you're just trying to get through the shift. My uncle Arthur, he used to fix clocks. Grandfather clocks, cuckoo clocks, you name it. His shop was downtown, right next to this old bakery that made the best rye bread. The smell of the caraway seeds would just drift right into his shop. He'd sit there with his little magnifying glass over his eye, working on these tiny gears. He told me once that time is just a way for the universe to keep everything from happening all at once. He was a smart guy, Arthur. Smoked a pipe, cherry tobacco. The smell of that tobacco and the rye bread... it's a smell I'll never forget. He left me one of his clocks when he passed, a mantle clock. It still chimes every hour, nice and clear. 

But yeah, the mood was better for maybe three or four months, but the system... the tracking... that never took a break.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient demonstrates persistent psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions about the routing system, auditory hallucinations of dispatch calls) lasting over 1.5 years, concurrent with a major depressive syndrome (pervasive sadness, hopelessness, low energy) lasting over 2 years. Critically, he confirms a distinct period of 3-4 months where his depressive symptoms fully remitted while the delusions and hallucinations persisted, establishing that psychotic symptoms occur independently of mood disturbance for a substantial period, satisfying the core diagnostic requirement for schizoaffective disorder. Since mood symptoms are present for the majority of the total illness duration and only depressive (not manic) episodes are described, this fits schizoaffective disorder, though the specific subtype (depressive type, F25.1) could not be further specified within the provided ICD-10 candidate list restricted to F25.9.
